summary: On Tuesday evening, an NBC4 news helicopter crashed between two commercial buildings in Chatsworth, killing three people, including a pedestrian on the ground, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.
The aircraft went down while covering a deadly collision involving a Metro bus and an SUV that occurred two hours earlier on Nordhoff Street, officials said.
Fifty-Six firefighters responded to the fiery wreckage, while NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams confirmed on air that the station had lost contact with its crew.
One additional person was transported to a hospital in unknown condition, while the National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration announced they will investigate the crash.
The crash renews scrutiny over aerial news gathering in Los Angeles, where helicopter coverage has long defined broadcast journalism and exposed reporters to inherent airspace risks.
title: Source Icon

summary: On Tuesday, the Senate blocked the Clarity Act after a procedural vote fell 50-49, far short of the 60 votes required to advance the comprehensive crypto market structure legislation.
Republican leaders released a revised version Sunday adding new ethics restrictions to address Democratic concerns, but those changes failed to resolve remaining opposition on Capitol Hill.

Following the vote, bitcoin prices dropped 3%, while Coinbase and Circle shares slid 8% and 10% respectively; Senator Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., told reporters earlier that "it's over" if the procedural vote failed.
Senators are scheduled to leave Washington in early October for the campaign recess, with midterm elections in seven weeks, while The House recesses even earlier, limiting time to revisit the bill.

The failed vote likely forces the crypto industry to wait until next year for clearer rules, as The SEC and CFTC continue shaping policy through enforcement and rulemaking rather than durable federal statute.
title: Senate cloture vote on Clarity Act fails, dealing regulatory blow to crypto industry

summary: Kennedy Center board members voted Tuesday to close the performing arts venue, citing "dire" financial and structural conditions amid an ongoing dispute over renaming the building for President Donald Trump .

Attempting to secure funding, the board previously voted to rename the facility "Trump Plaza," but Judge Christopher Cooper ruled the institution cannot install memorials for Trump without Congress's blessing.

Although the board claims the center is in a "dire" financial position, Judge Cooper noted the institution still has access to $257 million appropriated by Congress for necessary capital improvements.
Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, praised the court's ruling, stating the center is named for President Kennedy "and no one else," while accusing President Trump of holding the memorial hostage for vanity.

As the board threatens to keep the Kennedy Center closed for two years, legal disputes continue over whether the board can bypass statutory restrictions on renaming the site to resolve its fiscal crisis.
title: Kennedy Center board votes to immediately close venue for renovations

summary: On Tuesday, District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the Kennedy Center board from inscribing President Donald Trump 's name on the main building, ruling that such memorials require Congressional approval.
In May, Cooper declared the board's earlier renaming attempts unlawful, establishing that only Congress holds the power to change the facility's official designation.
The board claimed that recognizing Trump is necessary to secure his fiscal oversight and raise $100 million, even though Congress has already appropriated $257 million for renovations.

Following a ceiling collapse reported by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, the board shifted Tuesday's agenda to focus exclusively on the facility's "necessary closure" rather than additional Trump tributes.
The proposed closure faces resistance from Rep. Joyce Beatty's team, with lawyer Norm Eisen calling the plan "foolishness" and vowing to contest the board's efforts.
title: Judge blocks Kennedy Center board from putting Trump's name on plaza, building

summary: On Tuesday, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman announced that prosecutors will not seek the death penalty against Nick Reiner, charged with murdering his parents in December 2025.
Accused of murdering his father, Rob Reiner , and mother, Michele Singer Reiner, Nick was arrested nine months ago near the University of Southern California after the December killings.
Romy Reiner discovered the bodies after a massage therapist found no answer on Dec. 14; an indictment unsealed last month added an allegation of lying in wait to the charges.
Hochman consulted with the victims' loved ones, including the siblings, before deciding against the death penalty; Reiner now faces a maximum sentence of life without the possibility of parole.

Although the office considered the family's views in the final decision, Hochman did not disclose what specific punishment the family had requested for Reiner regarding the first-degree murder charges.
title: Nick Reiner prosecutors won’t seek death penalty in the killing of parents Rob and Michele Reiner, DA says

summary: On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed that Canada become the European Union's first "associate member" during her State of the European Union address in Strasbourg, France.

This overture follows a historic breakdown in Canada-U.S. trade relations last month, as President Donald Trump's tariffs and rhetoric about making Canada the 51st state pushed Ottawa to seek closer European ties.
Von der Leyen stated the EU and Canada will build on their existing CETA agreement by creating an "Alliance for the Future" aimed at establishing "a common prosperity and economic security space."
Receiving a standing ovation from European lawmakers on Wednesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to address the European Parliament on Thursday regarding this "unique alliance."
Responding to a "fracture in the international rules-based system," von der Leyen noted the partnership is "not against anyone else" to avoid antagonizing the United States.
title: EU opens door for Canada to become its first associate member, von der Leyen says

summary: On Tuesday, opening statements begin in the federal bribery trial of Ward 8 Council member Trayon White, following a diverse jury of 14 residents sworn in Monday after two days of selection.
Prosecutors allege White accepted $35,000 in bribes during 2024 to influence city contracts, eventually agreeing to kickbacks totaling $156,000; White has pleaded not guilty.

DOJ officials accused White of jury tampering earlier this month regarding social media posts, while his defense team argued his comments were lawful and his right to a "fair trial and a fair shake" was at risk.
The D.C. Council unanimously expelled White last year, though Ward 8 voters re-elected him months later; defense attorneys may call former D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine as a witness.
If convicted, White faces up to 15 years in prison and would automatically forfeit his council seat, as prosecutors plan to present their case over five days with FBI informant testimony.
title: Federal Corruption Trial Opens for DC Council Member Trayon White

summary: On Monday, former youth counselor Jeffrey Buskey faces trial for 21 counts of aggravated felonious sexual assault involving David Meehan, whose 2019 allegations sparked an unprecedented criminal investigation in New Hampshire .
Meehan filed the first of more than 1,100 lawsuits alleging abuse spanning six decades, triggering the arrest of Buskey and eight others and leading to a settlement fund for victims.

The Sununu Youth Services Center once housed upward of 100 children but now typically serves fewer than a dozen. Buskey denied the allegations, saying "I was always nice to the kid, I was always trying to help him."
A jury awarded Meehan $38 million in May 2024, though that verdict remains in dispute as the state seeks to reduce the judgment to $475,000.

Lawmakers have approved closing the Sununu Youth Services Center and replacing it with a smaller building in a new location. In separate criminal cases, Bradley Asbury, Stanley Watson, and James Woodlock have been convicted.
title: Ex-youth detention center counselor faces sex assault trial in New Hampshire

summary: On Wednesday, attorneys for the family of Charlie Kirk publicly released a notice of claim against Utah Valley University, alleging that security failures led to the CEO's fatal shooting on September 10, 2025.

Attorneys described the shooting as "entirely preventable," citing "reckless decisions" by UVU officials who failed to secure rooftops or establish a safe perimeter for the event attended by 3,000 people.

The notice alleges that UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long requested approval from then-UVU President Astrid Tuminez to allocate more than six officers—representing only 25% of the police force—but his request was denied.
This filing is a required legal step under Utah law to pursue a wrongful death lawsuit within two years, naming the State of Utah, the university, and former administrators as potential defendants.

Accused shooter Tyler Robinson remains in custody awaiting trial for aggravated murder, with a trial date expected at an October 23 hearing. The notice ensures the family can pursue a court remedy over the next year.
title: Family of Charlie Kirk plans suit against Utah university over alleged security lapses

Rogers' campaign released a statement alleging Raj displayed "bias and favoritism" toward El-Sayed and that his past comments were "inconsistent with the level of gravity" expected in a major Senate race.
El-Sayed criticized Rogers for dodging the event, arguing he lacked the "respect" to face voters and hard questions. The Democratic nominee stood alongside the empty podium during the broadcast.

Defending his neutrality on Good Day Detroit, Raj asserted, "nothing we do at this station is trying to take a side." Rogers has agreed to participate in two other upcoming debates scheduled for October.

Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat remains a highly competitive 2026 race with Republicans holding a 53-47 majority. Democrats need to gain four seats to retake U.S. Senate control, making each debate critical for voter outreach.
title: Rogers set to skip Michigan Senate debate over outlet’s ‘favoritism’ toward El-Sayed

summary: On Tuesday, FBI Director Kash Patel testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee, refusing to commit to keeping federal agents away from polling places during the midterm elections.

Amid President Donald Trump's repeated claims that the 2020 election was "Rigged," Democrats sought assurances that federal officials would follow the law, which carries a potential five-year prison sentence for violations.

Senator Peter Welch pressed Patel during the hearing, prompting the FBI director to state: "On election day, the FBI will follow the law. If there's a reason to go there because there's been a violation of the law, we will."
Election crimes coordinators are stationed across all 56 FBI field offices, Patel confirmed, maintaining that agents will respond to potential legal violations on Election Day.

Controversial hiring standard changes also drew scrutiny, with Patel defending the removal of automatic disqualifications for theft or bestiality, asserting the agency did not want to "punish victims of bestiality.
title: FBI Director Kash Patel Clashes with Senators Over Potential Presence of Agents at Voting Locations

United States military operations have focused on destroying Iran's nuclear and conventional military capabilities; a second phase aims to prevent rebuilding and maintain global stability.
The war has cost taxpayers $33.4 billion since February, while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returned to over 50% of normal levels despite remaining below pre-war volumes of roughly 20%.
Before heading to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last Wednesday, Trump claimed the war will end "immediately after the election" because Iran "can't hold out any longer."
Ongoing tit-for-tat strikes between United States and Iranian forces near the Strait have killed 18 servicemen and women, as military vessels continue patrolling the contested region.
title: JD Vance Says Iran War Could Enter ‘Much Different Phase’ Within Months

summary: On Tuesday, The Wilderness Society and Wilderness Workshop sued Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Wyoming Director Kris Kirby, alleging June oil and gas lease sales in Wyoming and Colorado threaten critical big game migration corridors.

Conducted under last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the contested sales covered 3,906 square miles in Wyoming and 430 square miles in Colorado, with The BLM collecting revenue through a 12.5% royalty rate.

Pronghorn herds in the leased areas range from about 37% to 66% below objectives, while mule deer herds are 25% to 62% below; a 14-year study indicates energy development in migration corridors curtails habitat use by about 39%.

The lawsuit asks the District Court to set aside the sales and return the issue to The BLM, which declined comment due to current litigation, after conservationists argued leases constitute an 'irreversible commitment.'

Disputing the lawsuit's central claims, Ryan McConnaughey, interim president of the Petroleum Association, stated the legal action 'mischaracterizes the federal oil and natural gas leasing process,' noting actual development requires additional BLM approvals.
title: Oil and Gas Leases Threaten Big Game Migration Routes, Lawsuit Claims

summary: On Tuesday, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a letter of intent at the Pentagon in Washington to deepen defense industry cooperation between weapons makers in both countries.

The agreement seeks to strengthen industrial ties between the two allies as defense inventories decline. Hegseth and Pistorius aimed to enhance weapons production capacity amid dwindling defense stocks.

Pistorius confirmed plans for a German purchase of Tomahawk cruise missiles, stating, "It's about coming closer together in those areas in which we need each other." Details still require finalization.

Germany and the United States remain "on the same page" regarding European security concerns, Pistorius said. U.S. officials expressed appreciation for Germany's accelerated efforts to increase defense spending and troops.

Pistorius emphasized that planned weapons purchases would not create excessive dependency on the United States, instead helping to balance the partnership. Officials continue working out cooperation specifics.
title: Germany, US sign agreement to deepen defense cooperation between industries

summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is expected to attend a state dinner for Chinese President Jinping in Washington next week, according to a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Tuesday.

Hosting a state dinner for Jinping is notable because Trump often characterizes China as a rival, despite such events typically being reserved for heads of allied nations. Trump previously held one state dinner this term for Britain's King Charles and Queen Camilla.
Huang previously traveled to China with Trump earlier this year. He attended a state dinner Jinping hosted for Trump in May, alongside SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Apple CEO Tim Cook.

A White House official told CNBC, "President Trump has invited several great American business leaders to his dinner with President Xi because he will always prioritize making good deals for our country." Other guests remain unconfirmed.

Artificial intelligence is expected to be a central topic of discussion when Xi meets with Trump. The United States and China lead in advancing AI technologies, and Nvidia supplies essential chips to AI developers, positioning the company as a key player in global discussions.
title: Nvidia CEO to attend Trump dinner for Xi: Report

This event follows Hegseth's controversial gathering last year at Marine Corps Base Quantico, where he stunned senior officers by declaring the military would no longer tolerate what he called 'beardos' or 'fat generals.'

Expanding the invite list to lower-ranking troops, the Pentagon also mandates attendees rank among top performers and demonstrate integrity and discipline, while selected service members will work out alongside Hegseth.

Critics argue the emphasis oversimplifies military capability and risks using service members as props for political messaging, while Hegseth has faced controversy for fitness changes intended to reduce women's eligibility.

Though the Pentagon declined to comment on selection criteria, Hegseth has framed his mission as 'fixing decades of decay,' prioritizing physical readiness as essential to military effectiveness in future conflicts.
title: Pentagon Wants Only the Fittest Troops to Attend Upcoming Hegseth Speech: Report

Responding to calls from rival AI leaders for coordinated pauses, Zuckerberg argued that user trust and alignment are key competitive differentiators, as consumers will reject misaligned or unreliable AI agents.
The Meta chief emphasized that potential legal liability serves as a powerful deterrent against releasing unsafe systems, giving labs direct motivation to prevent real-world harm.

Highlighting Meta's internal precautions, Zuckerberg cited the decision to delay the release of its "Muse" AI model for several months to strengthen safety safeguards and engage third-party evaluators.
Zuckerberg’s position directly counters recent appeals from Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI executives who urged industry-wide coordination to manage risks surrounding superintelligent systems.

summary: On Tuesday, the House voted 220-204 to restrict President Donald Trump 's military authority in Iran, marking a third symbolic rebuke of the ongoing conflict.
Since launching Feb. 28, the war has cost more than $38 billion and disrupted oil shipments, fueling public skepticism with 67% of voters saying military action hurt the United States.
Seven Republicans joined most Democrats in Tuesday's vote, an increase from prior efforts as lawmakers campaign with less than 50 days before November elections.
Although the House passed the measure, it faces uncertain prospects in the Senate, and Trump would almost certainly veto any legislation curtailing his military powers.
Republican Rep. Brian Mast argued Iran remains a threat and Trump is against "forever wars," while Democrats claimed the administration lacks a strategic resolution after seven months of fighting.
title: House votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on

summary: On Tuesday, the Congressional Budget Office reported the six-month U.S. war against Iran has cost about $38 billion, with expenses projected to rise by around $3 billion a month if the conflict continues.
Launched on February 28, the conflict has placed a significant financial burden on the Pentagon, driven primarily by the rapid drawdown of munitions and equipment losses sustained during operations.

Pentagon estimates placed costs at $33.4 billion as of June 29, including $7.4 billion in operating expenses and $22.3 billion to replace munitions; the Defense Department watchdog warned of "strategic inventory shortfalls."
Rising energy prices from Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea disruptions are expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in early 2027, according to the CBO, straining an already stretched federal budget.

Rebuilding missile-defense interceptors could take at least five years, the CBO warned, leaving the U.S. with reduced inventories that could prove "especially problematic" in conflicts with adversaries like China.
title: Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month, CBO says

summary: On Sunday, Council of Fashion Designers of America CEO Steven Kolb was filmed physically restraining two protesters during a runway show for Cos in New York, an incident that stunned the fashion world.
Video shows Kolb covering the mouths of Andrija Barak and Mason Melito while restraining them with his arms and legs, as the two were among six employees present to disrupt the show.
Moira Colley, senior director of media relations for PETA , said Tuesday the group initially planned to file a police report against Kolb but changed course after consulting with attorneys.
Kolb has apologized for his actions and is taking a leave from his CFDA role pending an investigation, though he has agreed to meet with the organization.
Advocates intend to show Kolb footage of sheep mistreatment to argue for ending wool use, hoping he will repeat his previous success in banning fur from runway shows.
title: PETA says it plans meeting with fashion executive who restrained protesters at NY Fashion Week

The RIS Network, described as an arm of the Russian Federation's apparatus, has conspired to conduct attacks and murders worldwide since at least 2024, prosecutors alleged in the indictment.
Recruiters offered $40,000 to 'eliminate' a U.S.-based Russian dissident, while a separate plot involved $25,000 to murder an individual in Lithuania, according to court documents.

summary: On Tuesday, the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas charged seven noncitizens with illegally voting or falsely claiming citizenship as part of a broader Trump administration focus on noncitizen voting.

President Donald Trump has pushed the Postal Service to restrict mail ballots to verified citizens, a plan the Supreme Court rejected Monday while the Justice Department sued for voter data in 30 states.
Those charged, ranging in age from 20 to 69, hold citizenship in Mexico, India, Nigeria, and Congo. Some voted or attempted to vote in the 2024 and 2018 general elections.

Attorney General Ken Paxton, running for Senate against Democrat James Talarico, received 117 referred cases for investigation after cross-checking federal databases with passport information and other agencies.
The seven charges represent a minute fraction of nearly 18 million registered voters in Texas. Research shows noncitizen voting remains rare, though the Trump administration claims it is widespread.
title: Federal charges announced in Texas are part of broader Trump focus on noncitizen voting

Right-Leaning coverage de-emphasizes the tally and advocacy, instead portraying college sports as a “Wild West” needing to be “rein in” through “guardrails” on NIL, transfers, and revenue sharing.
Center coverage bridges these views by stressing a possible later vote and naming critic Chris Murphy.

summary: The Senate voted 74-24 on Tuesday to advance the Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan measure establishing federal standards for college athletics amid a rapidly shifting legal landscape.
Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, stated the bill aims to quell "the chaos we have in college sports," warning that without federal action, athletic programs face jeopardy.

The legislation would double the salary cap to nearly $49 million per school while redefining third-party NIL deals, providing the NCAA limited lawsuit immunity and establishing national rules for recruiting and transfers.
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., argued the bill protects industry profits over athlete compensation, while the NAACP and labor groups raised concerns about athlete protections and NCAA accountability.
The measure must now navigate the House, where support remains unclear amid debate over transgender sports language, all within the Senate's final three weeks before November's elections.
title: Senate votes to advance bill to regulate college sports, athlete compensation

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Leon Black’s noncompliance as deliberate obstruction, using terms like “stonewalling,” “defied,” and “Epstein associate,” while highlighting his lawyers’ description of the resolution as “a complete abomination.” Right-leaning coverage emphasizes the investigative rationale—his testimony as “crucial” to tracing financial institutions’ ties to Epstein—alongside Black’s lawsuit challenging subpoena authority and the expected full House vote.
Center coverage, where present, uses restrained procedural language such as “declined to comply” and stresses the unanimous committee action.

summary: On Tuesday, the House Oversight Committee voted 41-0 to recommend holding billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying two subpoenas related to his financial relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein .

The inquiry stems from Black's $158 million in payments to Epstein for "tax and estate planning advice." After Black testified voluntarily in June but left early, the committee issued subpoenas for further information he failed to provide.

Black's attorneys, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, called the contempt markup a "complete abomination" and "retaliation." They argued the subpoenas were illegal and filed a lawsuit seeking to block the proceedings, citing an abuse of power.

With the committee's unanimous recommendation, the contempt resolution moves to the House floor, where Chairman James Comer expects a vote this week before lawmakers leave Thursday to campaign for the midterms.

Seeking to postpone the contempt resolution, Black's legal team filed a complaint Tuesday with the Office of Congressional Conduct, alleging Comer violated House rules and questioning the validity of the committee's proceedings.
title: House Oversight votes to hold Leon Black in contempt over Epstein deposition

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the episode as a morally serious issue involving a “violent AI video,” stressing Manning’s “insensitive” laughter, his apology’s “nothing funny” wording, and Holly Rowe’s reaction.

Right-Leaning coverage centers individual responsibility and backlash, saying Manning “screwed up,” “came under fire,” and portraying others’ laughter as “infuriating.” Center coverage is comparatively restrained, emphasizing a “fake video,” the apology, and postgame context, including Texas’s victory over Ohio State.
The pivotal divide is whether to foreground simulated violence against a female reporter or broaden condemnation to public behavior.
All perspectives agree the video was fabricated, Manning laughed, and he apologized, reflecting shared concern over accountability amid wider debates about online culture and personal conduct.
summary: On Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, Texas quarterback Arch Manning issued an apology on Instagram for laughing at an AI-generated video depicting Longhorns coach Steve Sarkisian slapping ESPN reporter Holly Rowe.

Following a Saturday night postgame incident where Sarkisian cut off Rowe's interview and walked away, internet users circulated the AI-generated video, which Manning initially called "hilarious" during his weekly press conference.

Reporters in the press conference room also joined Manning in laughter. In his apology, Manning wrote: "I specifically want to apologize to Holly Rowe for what she has personally had to deal with because of my comments."

Critics condemned Manning's reaction, emphasizing his status as nephew of Super Bowl-winning quarterbacks Peyton and Eli Manning. Both Manning and the reporter who shared the video have since issued public apologies.

Manning committed to change, stating: "I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward." The incident underscores broader concerns about online behavior and respect for media professionals.
title: Texas’s Arch Manning apologizes for laughing at AI video of coach slapping female reporter

Center coverage bridges these frames but adds the FAA’s 07:15–09:14 Texas window, calls the launch “high-stakes,” and describes SpaceX as “thundering ahead” and “proving the doubters wrong.” A key dividing line is the unresolved catch discrepancy: no booster catch versus a ship catch.

summary: On September 22, SpaceX plans to launch its 14th Starship flight, targeting an orbit attempt with a 75-minute launch window starting at 7:15 a.m. in Texas.
For this mission, SpaceX said Tuesday that it made "several modifications" to the booster's hardware and software to "address issues seen on the previous flight."
The super heavy lift rocket will carry 26 Starlink satellites into an orbit 275 km above Earth, completing six orbits over about 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean west of Chile.
If successful, this flight will generate revenue for SpaceX, marking the first orbital Starship mission as the company works to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets.
Founder and CEO Elon Musk aims to fly Starship "reliably several times per week" to save resources, though he recently walked back plans to use the launch tower to catch the upper stage.
title: SpaceX targets first Starship orbital test on September 22

summary: On Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that investigations handled by former federal prosecutor Joseph DiGenova will continue following DiGenova's resignation last week.

DiGenova had joined the Justice Department in April to lead a Florida-based investigation scrutinizing President Donald Trump 's political foes and seeking to establish that Trump was the victim of a long-running criminal conspiracy.

The investigation examines 2017 intelligence findings regarding Russia's 2016 election interference, as well as matters previously probed by former Special Counsel Jack Smith, including classified document retention at Mar-a-Lago.
Blanche expressed appreciation for DiGenova's work, stating, "we're not going to slow down just because somebody leaves," signaling continuity in the department's investigative efforts.
Despite the investigation's broad mandate to establish a conspiracy against the president, the probe has not resulted in any criminal charges to date.
title: US attorney general says probes handled by ex-prosecutor DiGenova will continue

summary: On Tuesday, 55-year-old businessman Alex Saab pleaded guilty in Miami federal court to one count of money laundering conspiracy, agreeing to forfeit $195 million and cooperate with U.S. investigators.

Admitting to an extensive bribery system, Saab confirmed the scheme "had the approval, participation and protection of some of the Venezuelan government's highest ranking public authorities" while utilizing shell companies to skim funds.
Former Gov. Jose Gregorio Vielma Mora received $17 million in kickbacks, and an individual identified as "Government Official 1A" designated a surrogate to receive bribe payments on their behalf.
Prosecutors may now use Saab as a witness against former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, who awaits a separate trial in New York on drug charges after being captured by U.S. Special Forces.

With Maduro's trial scheduled for June 1, 2027, the U.S. administration is simultaneously pivoting toward energy partnerships with entrepreneur Alejandro Betancourt to access oil fields holding 65 billion barrels of crude.
title: Maduro ally Alex Saab pleads guilty in a $195M money laundering case, agrees to cooperate

summary: A multistory building housing displaced families collapsed in Gaza City on Wednesday, killing at least 12 people and injuring 15, according to Shifa Hospital.
The structure had sustained significant damage during the Israel-Hamas war, and authorities had previously issued safety warnings regarding the building's condition.
Civil defense crews are searching for more than 60 missing people, utilizing bulldozers and manual labor to locate survivors despite a lack of heavy machinery.

Raed Al-Dahshan, director of the Gaza City civil defense service, said, "We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people," while at least four children were among the dead.

The local rescue service reports about 2,000 damaged buildings currently house families, with approximately 400 structures at risk of collapse, leaving displaced residents vulnerable to sudden structural failures.
title: At least 20 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses

summary: On Tuesday, The International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group released a report warning of a "near-total absence" of effective recourse for organizations facing de-banking due to alleged ties to terrorist financing.

The report argues de-banking is a predictable outcome of Canada's anti-terror financing framework, with Muslim-led charities and NGOs operating in Syria, Palestine, or Pakistan facing disproportionate impacts.
In one instance, a humanitarian organization operating in Syria received 15 to 30 days' notice before losing services, yet "No explanation of the underlying risk was given."
Financial institutions face no legal requirement to explain account closures, and no independent body in Canada reviews whether derisking decisions are non-discriminatory or evidence-based.
The group issued a dozen recommendations for structural reform and transparency; Tim McSorley, the monitoring group's national coordinator, said "We need to see concrete policy changes.
title: Action needed to ensure groups aren't unduly 'de-banked' over terror risks: report

summary: Military commanders from the United States, Israel, and several Arab nations convened in Germany last week for a closed-door meeting hosted by Central Command to address regional security amid ongoing conflict with Iran.
This gathering marked the first such meeting since the United States and Israel began the war against Iran more than six months ago, with escalating tensions over the Houthis driving the discussions.

Gen. Eyal Zamir met military chiefs from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt; Chief Admiral Brad Cooper organized the event to discuss deepening security cooperation.
Cooper confirmed American forces will remain in the Middle East despite recent Iranian attacks on bases, while presenting Washington's plan to expand vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Military ties have expanded since Israel signed the Abraham Accords in 2020 and shifted to CENTCOM's area of responsibility, with Israel providing intelligence and defense support to regional partners during the war.
title: CENTCOM hosted military chiefs from 8 countries in Germany, US official says

summary: On Tuesday, Vice President Vance stated the United States "cannot let our Middle Eastern foreign policy be subservient to the state of Israel," arguing Washington must prioritize national interests over automatic agreement.

Speaking during the All-In Podcast, Vance defended President Donald Trump's approach as grounded in national interests, comparing the relationship to NATO partnerships that do not require European policy subordination.

Vance has previously highlighted that interests can be "misaligned," citing June disagreements over Tehran policy, while acknowledging Israel as a key partner for intelligence and technology cooperation.
Christian Zionist advocate Heather Johnston immediately rejected the characterization, stating the United States is the world's superpower and has never been subservient to any other nation.

Supporters of the alliance face challenges as younger Americans grow increasingly skeptical, prompting Vance to argue advocates must explain why the partnership benefits the United States rather than relying on longstanding assumptions.
title: Vance Says U.S. Cannot Let Middle East Policy Be Subservient To Israel

Right-Leaning coverage also highlights “no choice,” but offers little summit, energy, or diversification context, leaving the decision’s sovereignty implications less explicitly developed rather than establishing a distinct counter-narrative.

Across perspectives, the shared focus is Canada ending the talks; the divergence lies in whether the episode underscores energy strategy, economic diversification, or simply the core decision.
summary: In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with the United States after a final effort collapsed, triggering 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on Canadian exports and retaliatory measures from Ottawa.
Former prime minister Stephen Harper endorsed the withdrawal at Canada 's national investment summit on Monday, stating the government had "no choice" but to walk away from U.S. trade negotiations.

Delivering closing remarks at the Toronto summit, Harper called the move "sad" but necessary, urging Canada to reduce reliance on the United States; Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic and Jean Chrétien attended.

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt ordered the province's public sector to stop purchasing American products when Canadian substitutes are available, citing the latest round of U.S. tariffs as justification.

A new report advocates rebooting domestic shipbuilding in Victoria to mitigate economic headwinds from the United States; building ferries in British Columbia would help the province weather harsh conditions ahead.
title: Harper says 'no choice' but to walk away from U.S. trade talks
